analysis.one_liner: Lets taxpayers and businesses elect a flat 17% tax and repeals the estate and gift taxes.
analysis.headline: The flat tax bill, backed by 11 House Republicans, never left the Ways and Means Committee and received no vote before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let any individual or business make an irrevocable choice to pay a flat tax of 19% for the first two years and 17% thereafter, instead of the normal income tax. A wage earner electing the flat tax would owe the rate on wages, retirement payouts, and unemployment benefits above a large standard deduction, with no tax credits allowed. The bill also repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes outright, and would require a two-thirds vote in each chamber to ever raise the flat rate or shrink the deductions. [S2][S3]
analysis.who_benefits: The biggest gains go to households with high incomes and large investment portfolios: the individual flat tax base covers only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment benefits, so interest, dividends, and capital gains would escape tax entirely for electors, and the top rate would fall from 35%+ to 17%. Owners of very large estates gain unconditionally from the repeal of the estate and gift taxes, which applies to all decedents and gifts after 2011 whether or not they elect the flat tax. Businesses also gain a 17% rate on active business income in place of the corporate tax. Filers with simple wage income get genuine simplicity. [S3]
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, capital owners, and large estates

how_it_helps.text: Individuals and businesses may make an irrevocable election to pay 19% for two years and 17% thereafter, in place of the regular income tax and the alternative minimum tax. [S2][S3]

The individual flat-tax base counts only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation above a standard deduction, leaving interest, dividends, and capital gains untaxed for electors. [S3]
Businesses electing the flat tax pay 17% (19% the first two years) on gross active business income minus the cost of business inputs and wages, replacing the corporate income tax. [S2][S3]
The bill repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes for decedents dying and transfers made after December 31, 2011. [S2][S3]
The standard deduction is large relative to current law ($30,320 for a joint return, plus $6,530 per qualifying child), and the amounts are adjusted for inflation. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and ultimately other taxpayers, bear the cost of the lost revenue: a 17% rate replacing rates up to 35%, a tax base that largely excludes investment income, and full repeal of the estate and gift taxes all reduce federal receipts. Wage earners who elect the flat tax lose every tax credit, including the earned income tax credit and child tax credit. Government agencies and tax-exempt employers (universities, hospitals, charities) would owe a new 17-19% tax on fringe benefits they provide employees, and state and local governments would lose estate tax revenue that flows back to states. Future Congresses would face a two-thirds supermajority requirement to raise the rate or trim the deductions. [S2][S3]

drawbacks.text: The estate and gift tax repeal applies to every large estate and gift after 2011, regardless of whether the taxpayer elects the flat tax; in 2011-2012 the estate tax applied only above roughly $5 million per person, so the benefit is concentrated among the wealthiest families. [S3]
Electors may claim no credits of any kind, which eliminates the earned income tax credit, child tax credit, and education and energy credits for anyone choosing the flat tax. [S3]

The bill requires a two-thirds vote in the House or Senate to increase the flat rate or reduce the standard deduction or business deductions, locking in the new rate structure beyond ordinary majority rule. [S2][S3]

Government agencies and tax-exempt organizations would owe a 17-19% tax on the value of fringe benefits provided to their employees, raising employment costs at universities, hospitals, charities, and federal, state, and local governments. [S3]

Cutting the top rate to 17%, taxing only wage income for electors, and repealing the estate and gift taxes would substantially reduce federal revenue, shifting the burden to other taxpayers through debt or spending cuts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for the bill is real simplicity: a filer with nothing but wages and a large standard deduction could replace a complicated return with a one-rate calculation. But the largest structural benefits — full repeal of the estate and gift taxes and a tax base that excludes interest, dividends, and capital gains — flow almost entirely to households at the top of the income and wealth distribution, while the lost revenue would have to be made up by everyone else. The two-thirds supermajority lock-in would make it unusually hard for a future Congress to undo the rate cuts. The design helps a little at the bottom of the wage scale and a great deal at the top.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and Rules Committees in March 2011, no hearing or markup was ever scheduled, and it died there when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

narrative.text: Representative Michael Burgess introduced the bill on March 11, 2011, joined by original cosponsors Representatives Bartlett, Cole, and Ross of Florida. [S3][S5]
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee and, for portions of its jurisdiction, to the Rules Committee. [S5]
No further action of any kind appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote. [S5]
The bill attracted 10 cosponsors, all Republicans, and none in the Senate. [S4][S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the progressive income tax, the estate and gift taxes, and the refundable tax credits all remained in place; the Treasury kept the revenue that the bill would have forfeited, and large estates continued to owe estate tax.

industries.note: The bill repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes for all large estates and gifts after 2011, a benefit that only applies to estates above several million dollars. It would also let high earners elect a 17% rate with investment income excluded from tax.

Money and financial instruments are excluded from the business tax base, and individual electors owe no tax on interest, dividends, or capital gains, so returns on financial wealth would go largely untaxed under the flat tax.

A business electing the flat tax pays 17% on active income minus inputs and wages, replacing the up-to-35% corporate rate; the gain comes at the cost of federal revenue that other taxpayers would make up.

Tax-exempt organizations and federal, state, and local government employers would owe a new 17-19% tax on the fringe benefits they provide employees, raising their cost of employing teachers, nurses, and public workers.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax planning industry
industries.note: A second, optional tax system alongside the existing one would create new election and planning work, even as a simpler flat tax could shrink routine preparation for filers who switch.
